reference.source: Neurogenetics and inherited metabolic disease references
clinicalPearls: CLN6 produces two distinct clinical pictures from the same gene: a variant late-infantile NCL of childhood and adult-onset Kufs disease type A, a progressive myoclonic epilepsy.
The late-infantile variant presents in early childhood with seizures, motor and language regression, ataxia, myoclonus and progressive visual loss.
Kufs disease type A causes progressive myoclonic epilepsy with dementia and ataxia but characteristically spares the retina, so vision is preserved, unlike the childhood NCLs.
It is caused by biallelic variants in CLN6, encoding an endoplasmic-reticulum transmembrane protein rather than a lysosomal enzyme.
Stored material accumulates as curvilinear, fingerprint and rectilinear profiles on electron microscopy and is rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase.
Because CLN6 is not enzyme-deficient, diagnosis depends on molecular genetics and enzyme assays are normal.
MRI shows cerebellar and then cerebral atrophy; adult Kufs type A may show predominantly cerebellar atrophy.
Kufs disease type A is CLN6-related, whereas Kufs disease type B is usually due to CTSF (CLN13), an important genetic distinction in adult NCL.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN6 disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in CLN6 on chromosome 15q23, encoding CLN6, a non-glycosylated transmembrane protein resident in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than the lysosome. CLN6 is not an enzyme; it acts together with CLN8 as part of a complex that recruits newly synthesised soluble lysosomal enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum and relays them towards the Golgi for onward lysosomal delivery. Loss of CLN6 function therefore impairs the supply of multiple lysosomal hydrolases, disturbing lysosomal degradation and causing accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, seen ultrastructurally as curvilinear, fingerprint and rectilinear profiles. The allelic spectrum explains the striking clinical range: some variants produce a childhood variant late-infantile NCL with retinal degeneration, whereas others cause adult-onset Kufs disease type A, a progressive myoclonic epilepsy with dementia in which the retina is spared.
additionalDifferentials: CLN5, CLN7 (MFSD8) and CLN8 variant late-infantile NCLs
Other adult progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Lafora disease, Unverricht-Lundborg disease, DRPLA, MERRF, sialidosis)
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing (CLN6 sequencing, NCL gene panel or exome sequencing), including in the adult Kufs work-up
Brain MRI for cerebellar and cerebral atrophy
EEG with photic stimulation for photoparoxysmal responses
Electroretinography and ophthalmology (childhood form; expected normal in Kufs type A)
Electron microscopy of skin, conjunctival or axillary biopsy for curvilinear and fingerprint profiles
Neuropsychometric assessment to characterise dementia in the adult form
Muscle, nerve or other targeted biopsy when excluding mimics
redFlags: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with cognitive decline in a young adult, raising Kufs disease type A
Developmental regression with visual loss in a child
Rapid loss of gait and coordination
reference.prognosis: Childhood CLN6 disease is relentlessly progressive with death typically in later childhood or adolescence; adult Kufs disease type A progresses more slowly but causes disabling myoclonus, dementia and premature death. Care is supportive.
pitfalls: Excluding NCL in an adult because vision is preserved; Kufs type A spares the retina.
Confusing Kufs type A (CLN6) with Kufs type B (CTSF/CLN13); they are genetically distinct.
Relying on enzyme assays, which are normal in CLN6.
Misattributing early childhood regression to an epileptic encephalopathy of unrelated cause.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so management is supportive across both the childhood variant and adult Kufs type A phenotypes

Control myoclonus and seizures of the progressive myoclonic epilepsy with agents such as valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam and piracetam-type drugs, avoiding sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine that worsen myoclonus
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and management of ataxia and spasticity for motor decline
Arrange ophthalmology and low-vision support in the childhood form, where vision is preserved in Kufs type A
Support nutrition and swallowing with gastrostomy feeding as bulbar function fails in the childhood form
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, rehabilitation and palliative care, with neuropsychology input for the dementia of the adult form
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
